note: Classical 面相 grounding (五行 element face, 三停 three courts, 五眼 five-eyes, per-feature descriptors), entertainment framing only. No health/medical/lifespan/financial claims (Backend §13). chunks.content: A Wood-element face — longer, upright and well-defined — is classically read in 面相 as upright, growth-minded and principled, a nature that reaches upward like a tree. Offered for reflection, not prediction.
A Fire-element face — pointed chin, broad forehead, animated features — traditionally signals passion, quick spirit and expressive warmth.
An Earth-element face — broad, full and grounded — is classically linked to steadiness, generosity and patient, dependable strength.
A Metal-element face — clear, defined and well-structured — is traditionally read as disciplined, precise and principled, with a cool composure.
A Water-element face — rounded, soft and full — is classically associated with adaptability, sociability and an easy, flowing warmth.
A Mixed-element face blends several elemental qualities — traditionally read as a versatile, many-sided nature not captured by one type.
An emphasised upper court (the forehead) is classically read in 三停 as an intellectual, reflective emphasis — a nature that leads with thought and vision.
Balanced three courts — forehead, midface and jaw in even proportion — are traditionally read as a harmonious, well-rounded temperament.
An emphasised lower court (jaw and chin) is classically linked to a grounded, practical and determined nature — strength that shows in action and will.
Narrow eye spacing is classically read in 五眼 as focus and precision — a nature attentive to detail and quick to concentrate.
Balanced eye spacing is traditionally read as even-handed perspective — a composed, well-proportioned outlook.
Wide eye spacing is classically linked to a broad, easygoing perspective — a nature that takes in the big picture and stays relaxed.
Straight eyebrows are classically read as a direct, rational temperament — clear-minded and matter-of-fact.
Curved eyebrows are traditionally linked to warmth and sociability — an approachable, people-attuned nature.
Arched eyebrows are classically read as expressiveness and poise — a flair for presence and a lively responsiveness.
Sparse eyebrows are traditionally read as an independent, understated spirit — someone who acts on their own counsel.
Thick, full eyebrows are classically linked to energy and conviction — a strong will and forthright vigour.
Round eyes are classically read in 面相 as openness and curiosity — an expressive, feeling-forward nature.
Almond eyes are traditionally linked to poise and balance — a composed, discerning presence.
Narrow eyes are classically read as focus and shrewdness — a watchful, considering nature.
Upturned eyes are traditionally linked to optimism and ambition — an upward, hopeful outlook.
Downturned eyes are classically read as gentleness and empathy — a kind, approachable warmth.
Deep-set eyes are classically read as depth and reserve — an observant, inward, considering nature.
Balanced-set eyes are traditionally read as an even, approachable presence — engaged without intensity.
Prominent eyes are classically linked to expressiveness and openness — a warm, outwardly engaged spirit.
A straight nose is classically read in 面相 as fairness and self-discipline — a steady, principled bearing.
An aquiline nose is traditionally linked to independence and drive — a strong-willed, self-directed nature.
A small, rounded nose is classically read as approachability and charm — an easygoing, personable warmth.
A broad nose is traditionally linked to groundedness and generosity — a sturdy, open-handed nature.
A full, fleshy nose tip is classically read in 面相 as warmth and enjoyment of life — a generous, sociable spirit.
A low nose bridge is classically read as adaptability and ease — a flexible, cooperative temperament.
A medium nose bridge is traditionally read as balance — self-possession without rigidity.
A high nose bridge is classically linked to independence and pride of purpose — a self-assured, autonomous streak.
A full mouth is classically read in 面相 as warmth and generosity — an expressive, affectionate nature.
A thin mouth is traditionally linked to precision and self-control — measured words and a disciplined manner.
A balanced mouth is classically read as even-tempered expression — warmth and restraint in fair measure.
Naturally upturned mouth corners are traditionally read as optimism and good humour — a bright, welcoming disposition.
Naturally downturned mouth corners are classically read as seriousness and depth — a thoughtful, composed bearing.
High-set ears are classically read in 面相 as quick intelligence and drive — an alert, ambitious cast of mind.
Balanced-set ears are traditionally read as even judgment — a steady, well-proportioned temperament.
Low-set ears are classically linked to a calm, deliberate nature — someone unhurried and grounded.
Small ears are classically read as sensitivity and refinement — an attentive, discerning nature.
Medium ears are traditionally read as balance — receptive and steady in equal part.
Large ears are classically linked in 面相 to boldness and generosity — an open, expansive spirit.
Without a pronounced 卧蚕 (the soft ridge beneath the eye), tradition reads a cool, composed expressiveness — warmth held quietly in reserve.
A slight 卧蚕 beneath the eyes is classically read as gentle charm and approachability — a soft, likeable warmth.
A prominent 卧蚕 (the 'silkworm' ridge below the eye) is traditionally linked to charisma and warmth — an engaging, affectionate presence people are drawn to.
